receptor.d: A protein a signal plugs into — like a lock that a specific key fits.

ligand.d: Any molecule that plugs into a receptor.

agonist.d: Something that switches a receptor ON.

antagonist.d: Something that blocks a receptor so it can't switch on.

enzyme.d: A protein that speeds up one specific chemical reaction in the body.

transporter.d: A doorway in the cell wall that moves a substance in or out.

hormone.d: A chemical messenger that travels in the blood to act on distant parts of the body.

neurotransmitter.d: A chemical messenger that carries signals between nerve cells.

mitochondria.d: Tiny power plants inside cells that turn food and oxygen into energy.

mitochondrial.d: Relating to mitochondria, the cell's power plants.

autophagy.d: The cell's recycling program — it breaks down and reuses damaged parts.

senescent.d: A worn-out "zombie" cell that won't die and leaks inflammation.

senescence.d: When cells become worn-out "zombies" that won't die and leak inflammation.

senolytic.d: A compound that clears out worn-out "zombie" cells.

transcription.d: Copying a gene so the cell can use its instructions.

gene expression.d: How much a particular gene is being used by the cell.

upregulate.d: To make more of something (turn it up).

upregulates.d: Makes more of something (turns it up).

downregulate.d: To make less of something (turn it down).

phosphorylation.d: Attaching a tiny chemical tag that switches a protein on or off.

kinase.d: An enzyme that switches other proteins on or off by tagging them.

half-life.d: The time it takes for half of a substance to clear from your blood.

bioavailability.d: How much of a dose actually reaches your bloodstream.

first-pass.d: The liver breaking down much of a swallowed dose before it reaches the body.

cortisol.d: The main stress hormone — useful in short bursts, harmful when high for long.

insulin.d: The hormone that moves sugar and nutrients from blood into cells.

insulin sensitivity.d: How well your cells respond to insulin; higher is healthier.

testosterone.d: The main male sex hormone; drives muscle, libido, and more.

oestrogen.d: A key sex hormone — important in both women and men.

estrogen.d: A key sex hormone — important in both women and men.

estradiol.d: The main form of oestrogen, a key sex hormone.

dht.d: A stronger form of testosterone that drives hair loss and prostate growth.

aromatase.d: The enzyme that turns testosterone into oestrogen.

glutathione.d: Your cells' master antioxidant — their built-in rust protection.

antioxidant.d: A molecule that neutralises cell-damaging "free radicals".

inflammation.d: The body's defence-and-repair response; harmful when it's constant.

lipolysis.d: The release of stored fat to be burned for energy.

thermogenesis.d: Producing body heat, which burns calories.

thermogenic.d: Something that makes the body produce heat and burn more calories.

glycogen.d: The stored form of carbohydrate in your muscles and liver.

triglycerides.d: A type of fat that circulates in your blood.

vasodilation.d: Widening of blood vessels, which increases blood flow.

sirtuins.d: Repair-crew enzymes that switch on longevity programs (they run on NAD+).

telomeres.d: The protective caps on the ends of your DNA that shorten with age.

peptide.d: A short chain of amino acids — essentially a mini-protein.

catabolic.d: Breaking tissue down — the opposite of building.

pituitary.d: A gland in the brain that controls many hormones, including growth hormone.

adrenal.d: Glands on your kidneys that release stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline.

leydig.d: The cells in the testicles that make testosterone.

protein synthesis.d: The process of building new protein, such as muscle.

growth factor.d: A signal that tells cells to grow, divide, or repair.

nuclear receptor.d: A receptor inside the cell that changes which genes are active.

nitric oxide.d: A gas your body makes that relaxes blood vessels so more blood flows.

randomised controlled trial.d: The gold-standard experiment: people randomly get the real thing or a dummy.

in vitro.d: An experiment done in a dish, not in a living body.

in vivo.d: An experiment done in a living body.

acetylcholine.d: The brain chemical central to memory, focus, and muscle contraction.

cholinergic.d: Relating to acetylcholine, the memory-and-focus chemical.

adrenergic.d: Relating to adrenaline and noradrenaline — the fight-or-flight chemicals.

dopamine.d: The brain chemical behind motivation, reward, and focus.

serotonin.d: The brain chemical behind calm, mood, and contentment.

noradrenaline.d: An alertness-and-arousal brain chemical (also called norepinephrine).

myostatin.d: A protein that limits how much muscle you can build — the body's "stop growing" brake.

carnosine.d: A molecule in muscle that soaks up the acid ("the burn") during hard effort.

adenosine.d: The molecule that builds up during the day and makes you feel tired.

ghrelin.d: The hunger hormone — it makes you feel hungry.

amylin.d: A gut hormone that signals fullness, working alongside insulin.

prolactin.d: A hormone that, when too high, lowers libido.

methylation.d: Background chemistry the body uses to run DNA, mood, and detox.

homocysteine.d: A molecule that's harmful to blood vessels when it builds up too high.

cytokines.d: Messenger molecules the immune system uses to drive inflammation.

leukotrienes.d: Inflammatory messengers that drive some joint pain.

beta-glucans.d: Special sugars from mushrooms and yeast that "train" the immune system.

satellite cells.d: Muscle stem cells that repair and grow muscle fibres.

aromatisation.d: The conversion of testosterone into oestrogen.

osteoarthritis.d: The common "wear-and-tear" form of joint arthritis.

cofactor.d: A helper molecule (often a mineral) an enzyme needs to work — e.g. magnesium.

substrate.d: The raw material an enzyme acts on.

translation.d: Building a protein from the RNA copy of a gene.

pharmacokinetics.d: What the body does to a drug — absorb, distribute, metabolise, excrete.

pharmacodynamics.d: What the drug does to the body — its effects and how strong they are.

therapeutic index.d: The gap between an effective dose and a toxic one — bigger is safer.

cyp450.d: Liver enzymes that break down most drugs — the source of many interactions.

rct.d: Randomised controlled trial — the gold standard for proving a human effect.

meta-analysis.d: A study that pools many trials for the strongest overall answer.

placebo.d: An inert dummy treatment used to see if an effect is real.

tolerance.d: Needing more over time for the same effect, as the body adapts.

selectivity.d: How specifically a molecule hits its intended target and not others.

affinity.d: How tightly a molecule binds its target.

gpcr.d: G-protein-coupled receptor — the biggest receptor family; many drugs act here.

mtor.d: A master growth switch — on = build (muscle), off = repair/cleanup (autophagy).

ampk.d: A cellular “low-fuel” sensor that boosts fat-burning and mitochondria.

atp.d: The body’s energy currency, spent and remade constantly.

nmda receptor.d: A glutamate receptor central to learning, memory and excitation.

hpa axis.d: The brain–adrenal stress circuit that controls cortisol.

glycation.d: Sugar sticking to proteins and stiffening them — ages collagen and vessels.

shbg.d: A blood protein that binds sex hormones; more SHBG = less free testosterone.

ionotropic.d: A receptor that IS the channel — the signal opens a hole and ions pour through in milliseconds. The fast kind.

metabotropic.d: A receptor that is NOT a channel — it starts a chain of messengers inside the cell, so it acts over seconds and tunes rather than fires.

allosteric.d: Acting on a second site on a receptor, away from the main one — so it turns the volume up or down instead of switching it on.

orthosteric.d: Acting on a receptor's main site — the one the body's own molecule uses.

positive allosteric modulator.d: A molecule that cannot switch a receptor on by itself, but makes the body's own signal hit harder when it arrives.

partial agonist.d: Switches a receptor on, but only part way — it cannot produce a full effect no matter how much is present.

inverse agonist.d: Pushes a receptor below its resting activity — the opposite of switching it on, not merely blocking it.

modulator.d: A molecule that changes how strongly a receptor responds, instead of switching it on or off.

presynaptic.d: On the sending side of the gap between two nerve cells.

postsynaptic.d: On the receiving side of the gap between two nerve cells.

synapse.d: The tiny gap where one nerve cell passes a chemical message to the next.

vesicle.d: A small bubble inside a cell that stores a chemical messenger until it is released.

reuptake.d: Vacuuming a released messenger back into the cell that sent it, ending the signal.

transporter protein.d: A doorway in the cell wall that carries one specific substance in or out.

subunit.d: One of several protein pieces that snap together to build a receptor — swap one piece and the whole thing behaves differently.

isoform.d: One of several slightly different versions of the same protein, often doing the same job in different tissues.

voltage-gated.d: A channel that opens when the electrical charge across the cell wall changes.

ligand-gated.d: A channel that opens when a specific molecule docks onto it.

ion channel.d: A gated hole in the cell wall that lets charged particles through.

pore.d: The hole down the middle of a channel that ions actually travel through.

depolarisation.d: The cell's charge swinging toward zero — the electrical step that means "fire".

hyperpolarisation.d: The cell's charge pushed further from firing — the electrical step that means "stay quiet".

conductance.d: How easily charge flows through an open channel — the width of the tap, not how long it is open.

gradient.d: A difference in concentration or charge between two sides of a wall — the stored energy that makes things move on their own.

tonic.d: A steady background level that is always on.

phasic.d: Arriving in short bursts rather than as a steady level.

excitatory.d: Pushing a nerve cell toward firing.

inhibitory.d: Pushing a nerve cell away from firing.

excitotoxicity.d: Damage from too much excitation — a cell driven so hard it injures itself.

astrocyte.d: A support cell in the brain that cleans up spent messengers and recycles them.

long-term potentiation.d: A synapse getting durably stronger after being used hard — the cellular version of "it stuck".

plasticity.d: The nervous system's ability to rewire itself with use.

desensitisation.d: A receptor going quiet while a signal is still present, so the same signal stops working.

downregulation.d: The cell building fewer receptors because a signal has been too loud for too long.

upregulation.d: The cell building more receptors because a signal has been too quiet for too long.

second messenger.d: A molecule made inside the cell that carries a signal onward after the receptor has been hit.

g-protein.d: The relay switch a slow receptor flips on its inside face to pass the message along.

adenylate cyclase.d: The enzyme that makes cAMP, the most common inside-the-cell messenger.

phosphodiesterase.d: The enzyme that destroys inside-the-cell messengers — block it and the signal lasts longer.

cascade.d: A chain of switches where each step turns on the next, so a small signal becomes a large response.

nucleus.d: The compartment holding the cell's DNA — a signal has to reach it to change which genes run.

cytoplasm.d: The fluid interior of a cell, outside the nucleus.

membrane.d: The oily wall around a cell — nothing crosses it without a door.

lysosome.d: The cell's acid recycling bin, where worn-out parts are broken down for reuse.

proteasome.d: The cell's shredder for proteins that have been tagged for disposal.

ubiquitin.d: The tag a cell attaches to a protein to mark it for shredding.

mitophagy.d: Recycling worn-out power plants specifically — autophagy aimed at mitochondria.

apoptosis.d: A cell shutting itself down cleanly and on purpose, without spilling its contents.

inflammaging.d: The slow, low-grade inflammation that builds with age even without an injury or infection.

oxidative stress.d: More cell-damaging fragments being produced than the cell can mop up.

free radical.d: A molecule missing an electron, which rips one off whatever it touches.

cytokine.d: A messenger molecule the immune system uses to turn inflammation up or down.

clearance.d: How fast the body removes something — the emptying rate, not the amount present.

metabolite.d: What a substance becomes after the body has worked on it — sometimes inactive, sometimes the part that does the job.

cyp3a4.d: The single busiest drug-breaking enzyme in the liver — the usual reason two substances interfere with each other.

negative feedback.d: The output of a system switching off its own trigger — how the body holds a level steady.

hypothalamus.d: The brain's control panel for hormones, hunger, temperature and stress.

glucocorticoid.d: The class of stress hormones cortisol belongs to.

androgen.d: A male-type sex hormone — testosterone is the best known.

fsh.d: Follicle-stimulating hormone — the pituitary's instruction to make sperm or mature an egg.

luteinising hormone.d: The pituitary's instruction to the testes or ovaries to make sex hormones.

leydig cell.d: The cells in the testes that actually make testosterone.

melanocortin.d: A family of brain signals that link appetite, skin pigment and sexual arousal.

monoamine.d: The family of brain messengers that includes dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline.

ssri.d: A class of antidepressant that slows serotonin's removal from the synapse.

maoi.d: A class of drug that blocks the enzyme which destroys dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline.

muscarinic.d: The slow family of acetylcholine receptors — the ones that govern glands, gut and heart rate.

nicotinic.d: The fast family of acetylcholine receptors — the ones that fire muscle and sharpen attention.

endothelium.d: The single-cell lining inside every blood vessel, which decides how wide the vessel sits.

insulin resistance.d: Cells responding weakly to insulin, so the body has to shout louder to get the same effect.

glut4.d: The glucose doorway that muscle and fat cells move to the surface when insulin or exercise tells them to.

beta-oxidation.d: Chopping a fat molecule into fuel, two carbons at a time.

ketone.d: A fuel the liver makes from fat when carbohydrate is scarce, which the brain can burn.

mtorc1.d: The build-mode half of mTOR — the switch that turns fuel and protein into new tissue.

mtorc2.d: The other half of mTOR, which handles insulin signalling and cell shape rather than growth.

threshold.d: The level a signal has to pass before anything happens at all.

binding site.d: The specific pocket on a protein that a molecule has to fit for anything to happen.

eccentric.d: The lowering half of a lift, where the muscle is producing force while getting longer.

concentric.d: The lifting half, where the muscle produces force while shortening.

isometric.d: Holding a position — force with no movement.

moment arm.d: How far a muscle's pull sits from the joint it turns — the length of its spanner. Longer arm, more turning force for the same pull.

active insufficiency.d: A muscle crossing two joints cannot shorten fully at both at once — so it goes weak at one end when the other is already folded.

length-tension.d: A muscle's force depends on how stretched it is — too short or too long and it produces less.

sarcomere.d: The smallest repeating unit of a muscle fibre — the piece that actually shortens.

actin.d: The thin filament in muscle that the thick filament pulls on.

myosin.d: The thick filament in muscle whose heads grab and pull the thin one.

cross-bridge.d: One grab-pull-release cycle between the two filaments — the atom-scale event that is a contraction.

motor unit.d: One nerve plus every muscle fibre it commands — the smallest thing you can switch on.

innervation.d: Which nerve supplies a muscle, and therefore what happens when that nerve is injured.

proprioception.d: Your sense of where your own limbs are without looking.

muscle spindle.d: A stretch sensor inside a muscle that triggers a protective contraction when pulled fast.

golgi tendon organ.d: A tension sensor in the tendon that tells a muscle to let go before it tears.

stretch-shortening cycle.d: Stretching a muscle immediately before shortening it, so stored elastic energy adds to the effort.

slow-twitch.d: Fatigue-resistant muscle fibres built for long, low effort.

fast-twitch.d: Powerful muscle fibres that produce force quickly and tire quickly.

hypertrophy.d: Existing muscle fibres getting thicker — how muscles actually grow.

atrophy.d: Muscle fibres getting thinner from disuse or illness.

biarticular.d: Crossing two joints, so what happens at one changes what the muscle can do at the other.

proximal.d: Nearer the middle of the body — the shoulder end of an arm.

distal.d: Further from the middle of the body — the hand end of an arm.

supination.d: Turning the forearm so the palm faces up.

pronation.d: Turning the forearm so the palm faces down.

glenohumeral.d: The ball-and-socket shoulder joint itself, as distinct from the shoulder blade sliding on the ribs.

valgus.d: A joint collapsing inward — knees drifting toward each other.

aponeurosis.d: A flat sheet of tendon that spreads a muscle's pull over a wide area.

mechanical tension.d: The pulling force on a muscle fibre — the signal that actually tells it to grow.

time under tension.d: How long a muscle spends producing force in a set.

delayed onset muscle soreness.d: The ache that peaks a day or two after unfamiliar work. It measures novelty, not progress.
